articles.title: Your Prettiest Dashboard Is Lying to You (And Grafana Will Never Tell You)
articles.excerpt: Pull up a chair, grab a cup of chai, and let’s talk about the prettiest graph on your big screen. It might be completely empty. Somewhere right inside your team’s Grafana setup, there is a panel that…
articles.body: Pull up a chair, grab a cup of chai, and let’s talk about the prettiest graph on your big screen. It might be completely empty. Somewhere right inside your team’s Grafana setup, there is a panel that has not drawn a single real data point for six months. No bright red banners. No screaming error messages. Nothing. The graph line is dead flat, the legend at the bottom is blank, and whenever a sev-1 (severity-1, drop-everything) incident breaks out at 2:00 AM, everyone glances at that wall of monitors and breathes a sigh of relief: “Look, the payment error rate is zero! System is calm.” The system is not calm, my friend. The query is dead. The metric name it asks for simply does not exist anymore.

articles.body: In Part 1 , we looked at what happens when a single bad write hits your database: how Aurora Backtrack can rewind it, how idempotency stops the same request from running twice, and why a restored database quietly leaves behind the data written during the restore. Part 2 zooms out to the questions every team eventually has to answer: How much data can we afford to lose, and how long can we afford to be down? How does DynamoDB Point-in-Time Recovery actually work? Can we let automation detect a disaster and restore the database on its own? Which of the four AWS disaster recovery strategies should we pick? I will be honest: some of my first answers to these questions were wrong.

articles.title: The Margin Layer — Or, "It Passed" Is Not the Same as "It Was Nowhere Near Failing"
articles.excerpt: A nightly job finishes in 41 minutes against a 90-minute window. That is a pass. Two years later the same job finishes in 88 minutes against the same window. That is also a pass, reported the same way…
articles.body: A nightly job finishes in 41 minutes against a 90-minute window. That is a pass. Two years later the same job finishes in 88 minutes against the same window. That is also a pass, reported the same way, on the same green tile, by the same dashboard. The job did not get worse, exactly. It grew: more tenants, more rows, one more index, a partition scheme that stopped being optimal at some point nobody can name. What disappeared was not correctness. It was the margin — the distance between what the system does and the point where it stops working. Pass/fail collapses a distribution into a single bit, and the bit is the same for a measurement that is comfortably inside the limit and one that is one migration away from it.

articles.title: Linux nosymfollow blocks one symlink path, not every path problem
articles.excerpt: Linux nosymfollow blocks one symlink path, not every path problem Linux 5.10 added the MS_NOSYMFOLLOW mount flag. The option prevents symbolic links on a mount from being followed. It is a focused con…
articles.body: Linux nosymfollow blocks one symlink path, not every path problem Linux 5.10 added the MS_NOSYMFOLLOW mount flag. The option prevents symbolic links on a mount from being followed. It is a focused control for content roots, upload directories, and other file trees where a symlink should never become an escape route. It is also easy to overstate. What the mount option changes The mount(2) manual lists MS_NOSYMFOLLOW as a per-mount-point flag since Linux 5.10. statfs(2) exposes the corresponding ST_NOSYMFOLLOW flag. The mount option tells path resolution not to follow symbolic links on that mounted filesystem. The narrow scope is the important part. The option applies to the mount. A path that crosses into another mount may encounter different behavior.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 8, 2005: Europe launches Venus Express, its first mission to Venus
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. Here's why Venus Express mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 8, 2005, Europe launched its first mission to Venus. The spacecraft was called Venus Express. Venus is a hothouse planet, one where the atmospheric pressure can easily crush an unprotected spacecraft. Even from orbit, Venus Express had to survive harsh radiation. But the spacecraft lasted for more than nine years. During that time, Venus Express saw a weird vortex swirling around Venus's south pole . It also saw possible signs of active volcanoes . Venus Express also discovered that the planet generates its own auroras . These auroras happen when particles from the sun hit charged particles in the atmosphere. Late in the Venus Express mission, controllers told the spacecraft to dip down into Venus's clouds — even though the spacecraft wasn't designed to do this.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.
